CausalChain: Chronic liver damage → altered bile acid metabolism and increased intestinal permeability → dysbiosis of the gut microbiome → aberrant production of microbial metabolites and inflammatory mediators → impaired hepatocyte function (reduced albumin synthesis and bilirubin clearance) → worsened ALBI grade → poorer HCC prognosis and reduced efficacy of systemic therapies
Hypothesis: Modulating the gut microbiome (via probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal microbial transplantation) in patients with HCC can enhance hepatocyte function by restoring bile acid homeostasis and reducing inflammation, thereby improving the ALBI grade and leading to better clinical outcomes and improved responses to systemic therapies.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) arises in a setting of chronic liver damage where liver functional reserve is essential for guiding therapeutic decisions. The albumin‐bilirubin (ALBI) grade has emerged as a promising, objective marker of hepatic function in HCC and is correlated with outcomes following various treatment modalities. Recent evidence suggests that factors beyond direct hepatocyte injury, such as alterations in bile acid metabolism and chronic inflammation, could affect both albumin synthesis and bilirubin clearance. In parallel, an increasing body of literature implicates the gut microbiome in modulating bile acid profiles and impacting liver homeostasis. Here, we propose a novel hypothesis that gut microbiome composition directly influences the ALBI grade by modulating hepatocyte function via bile acid metabolism and inflammatory signals. In turn, therapeutic modulation of the gut microbiome may improve the ALBI grade and subsequently enhance responses to systemic treatments, including immune checkpoint inhibitors. This hypothesis provides a rationale for integrating microbiome‐targeted interventions into the management of HCC to potentially improve liver function and clinical outcomes.
